source_user: Contrast continuous batching with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Without continuous batching, a fixed batch commonly retains slots for finished requests until the remaining longest request completes, unless another packing policy intervenes. Continuous batching instead removes completed sequences and admits waiting ones at decode iteration boundaries. Mechanism: dynamic membership lets new work share subsequent iterations with survivors, reducing padding or idle capacity caused by unequal output lengths. Boundary: the benefit is workload-dependent and can disappear at low load or equal lengths; at saturation, KV-memory pressure and admission queueing may worsen latency. Use the same arrival and length distributions and report throughput together with TTFT, inter-token latency, queue time, p95/p99 latency, memory, and failures.
risks: Static batching semantics differ across runtimes, weakening attribution if undefined.
Higher utilization may trade against fairness or tail latency.
evidence_required: Explicit baseline and policy definitions, identical workload/configuration manifests, batch traces, repeated request-level metrics, memory telemetry, and failure accounting.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with continuous batching. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Two trade-offs are (1) queueing and fairness: admitting replacements can keep utilization high while increasing waiting time or starving long requests under an aggressive scheduler; and (2) memory pressure: each active sequence needs KV-cache storage, so admission may trigger eviction, paging, rejection, or OOM and erase throughput gains. Mechanism: the scheduler changes batch membership at iteration boundaries and reuses freed slots. Boundary: results depend on arrival rate, length distribution, scheduler policy, and KV capacity; continuous batching is not intrinsically faster. Test controlled loads and record admission/retirement, queue time, per-request latency tails, throughput/goodput, occupancy, memory, evictions, and errors.
risks: Average tokens/s may conceal starvation and p99 latency harm.
Memory failures can change the admitted population and bias comparisons.
evidence_required: Scheduler traces, per-request wait/service times, length/load sweeps, KV allocation and eviction/OOM logs, throughput, latency percentiles, and failure counts.

source_user: Explain how continuous batching interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Continuous batching can raise utilization and throughput for heterogeneous-length traffic by admitting queued requests when others finish, rather than holding a fixed batch slot. The trade-off is that more simultaneous sequences consume KV-cache memory and may add queueing or scheduler overhead. Boundary: at low load, equal lengths, or a memory-limited workload, the gain may be negligible or negative. Cache capacity and paging can change the active population.
